newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-The euro after the French election-DG Bank.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-The euro after the French election-DG Bank.

text.p: By Sabine Bohn, equities analyst and Ulrich Jochheim, bond analyst, at the DG Bank in Frankfurt

The socialists under their party leader Jospin emerged as the clear victors in the second round of the parliamentary elections in France last Sunday. President Chirac's plan to confirm the coalition formed by the Gaullist RPR party and the liberal UDF party for the remaining five years of his (first) presidential term thus did not work.

As the socialists with 253 seats did not attain the 289 seats needed for an absolute majority, they will probably have to rely on the support of the communists on important issues, who achieved a very good result of 38 seats.

The new Prime Minister Jospin will present his cabinet over the next few days, although according to Fifth Republic tradition the president has a de-facto veto right over the filling of certain positions, particularly in the areas of foreign and defence politics.

The filling of the post of foreign minister will be followed with particular interest, though at the moment former Prime Minister Michel Rocard, who was at university with Chirac, is seen as having a good chance. Former European Commission President Delors, who embodied the Socialists' credibility in European politics during the election campaign, will probably only have an advisory role.

His line is best characterised by his remark that one must talk firmly to the Germans as that is the only language they understand. Delors will also have had considerable influence on the European policy demands made by the Socialists in the election campaign: The Socialists not only want Italy and Spain to join EMU immediately and a European economic government in addition to the central bank, but also a "solidarity and growth pact" instead of the present "austerity pact".

In the face of the timetable for European politics (the state and government leaders' summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17 for example), the last point holds the greatest potential for conflict in the short term. The situation is also aggravated by the fact that the demands presented by the Socialists in the election campaign have been taken over by the most popular politician of the right, the former parliamentary president Seguin.

In addition, in the course of the continued discussion surrounding the time for the revaluation of the Bundesbank's gold reserves, Italy's chances of being one of the founding members of EMU have significantly increased.
Under these circumstances it will be difficult for the German government to assure the German public and the capital markets in a credible way that the euro will be as stable as the mark.
This also explains the rekindling of the delay discussion which seemed to end abruptly with German Chancellor Kohl's statement that he would stand again in the 1998 elections.

Under these circumstances it is not surprising that the US dollar and the British pound have once again significantly gained in value, as Asian investors in particular can barely understand the continuing EMU discussions.

Despite the confused situation we think that EMU delay is the less likely alternative: Firstly the Maastricht Treaty sets the 1.1.1999 as the latest possible start date, which it will be difficult to alter without the agreement of all the partners.

Secondly the German and the French side have invested a great deal of political capital in EMU and have general political motives for wanting the project's realisation, which also explains the US administration's support.

Only the so-called "empty shell theory" in which the EMU starts on schedule on 1.1.1999, but without members, has a certain charm. The EU member states would have the possibility to wait for a moment that was opportune not simply for economic reasons for the definite start of monetary union: The German government holding office could then prevent an EMU discussion in the coming election campaign and the French government could prevent greater strike and protest waves breaking out again due to broken election campaign promises.
German bond market

As the domestic policy problems arising from the coming 1998 budget are likely to continue at least until the beginning of July, we believe the upward potential of the German bond market to be very limited at the moment. Furthermore the discussions on the international financial markets surrounding a possible rise in key interest rates in the USA are likely to increase again prior to the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on July 1st.
German stock market

The result of the election and the political changes in France place no initial pressure on the German stock market. Quite the opposite: Share prices rose unexpectedly strongly on the 2.6.97, as the most recent election result strengthened the probability of a weak euro.

The dollar strength resulting from this supports our scenario of a continuing economic recovery driven by exports. There is therefore no risk for our equity forecasts. We are keeping to our DAX goal of 3,700/3,800 points by September 1997. By the end of the year we see the DAX at 3,450/3,550 points due to the expected interest rate rise in the second half of the year.
